prompt: A Senate committee votes to order an AI security bill reported. Which statement best describes that action?

options.text: The committee has recommended the bill for Senate consideration.
options.explanation: Committee approval advances the measure toward the chamber; it is not Senate passage.

options.text: The full Senate has approved the bill.
options.explanation: The committee is a subset of senators; chamber passage is a separate action.

options.text: The House must now vote on the bill.
options.explanation: The Senate has not yet passed and sent this bill to the House.

options.text: The bill now creates binding duties for developers.
options.explanation: Committee action alone does not enact a federal law.

hint: Think about which body actually took the vote.
takeaway: Always identify the decision-making body before interpreting a legislative milestone.

sources.title: CRS: Introduction to the Legislative Process

prompt: A committee hears testimony from AI company executives about model theft. What can you conclude from the hearing alone?

options.text: The executives’ recommendations will become statutory text.
options.explanation: Testimony can influence drafting, but Congress is not required to adopt it.

options.text: The committee is gathering information; passage of a bill is not established.
options.explanation: A hearing can inform oversight or legislation without producing a markup or vote.

options.text: A model-security bill has passed the committee.
options.explanation: Hearing testimony is distinct from the committee action used to report legislation.

options.text: A model-security bill must already have been introduced.
options.explanation: A legislative hearing may occur before a bill is introduced.

hint: A hearing and a markup serve different functions.
takeaway: A hearing signals attention; check later actions to learn whether legislation advanced.

sources.title: CRS: Types of Committee Hearings

prompt: All 100 Senate seats are filled. On an ordinary AI bill subject to the usual legislative cloture rule, 58 senators vote for cloture. What is the result?

options.text: The bill is defeated on final passage.
options.explanation: This vote concerns limiting consideration, not final passage of the bill.

options.text: The bill passes because more than half support cloture.
options.explanation: Voting to limit consideration does not enact or pass the underlying bill.

options.text: Cloture is not invoked; the usual threshold is 60.
options.explanation: Three-fifths of senators duly chosen and sworn is 60 in this scenario.

options.text: Cloture is invoked because 58 is a simple majority.
options.explanation: The ordinary legislative cloture threshold is higher than a simple majority.

hint: This is a vote on limiting consideration, not on final passage.
takeaway: Distinguish the vote required to reach a decision from the vote on the decision itself.

sources.title: Senate: About Filibusters and Cloture

prompt: Debate has ended and the Senate votes on final passage of an ordinary AI bill. No special supermajority requirement applies. With a quorum present, what is generally required?

options.text: Three-fifths of all senators duly chosen and sworn.
options.explanation: That is the usual legislative cloture threshold, not the ordinary final-passage threshold.

options.text: Two-thirds of all senators duly chosen and sworn.
options.explanation: Ordinary legislation does not carry this general final-passage requirement.

options.text: Consent from every senator present.
options.explanation: Unanimous consent is a separate procedural route; it is not required for this vote.

options.text: A simple majority of senators voting.
options.explanation: Ordinary final passage generally requires a simple majority once procedural hurdles are cleared. If senators divide equally, the Vice President may cast a tie-breaking vote.

hint: The prompt says debate has ended and no special threshold applies.
takeaway: The shorthand “bills need 60 votes” can hide the distinction between cloture and passage.

sources.title: Senate: About Voting

prompt: The Senate passes an AI bill by unanimous consent, with no roll-call vote. Which description is supported by that record?

options.text: No senator objected to the request; there is no individual roll-call tally.
options.explanation: Unanimous consent operates through the absence of objection, not a recorded vote by every senator.

options.text: Every senator individually cast a recorded yea vote.
options.explanation: Unanimous consent is not a roll call recording each senator’s vote.

options.text: The bill failed because no vote total was recorded.
options.explanation: A measure can pass by unanimous consent without a numerical roll-call result.

options.text: Each senator endorsed every provision in a public statement.
options.explanation: The procedure does not establish individual public statements or motives.

hint: “No objection” and “100 recorded yeas” describe different evidence.
takeaway: Use the actual voting method when describing a legislator’s record.

sources.title: Senate: About Voting

prompt: Why might supporters try to include a qualifying AI-related tax provision in a budget reconciliation bill?

options.text: Reconciliation makes the President’s signature legally unnecessary in every case.
options.explanation: Reconciliation legislation follows the constitutional enactment process.

options.text: Senate debate on reconciliation is limited, avoiding the usual need for cloture.
options.explanation: Reconciliation offers expedited Senate consideration for eligible budgetary legislation.

options.text: Reconciliation bills can become law without House approval.
options.explanation: Both chambers must still approve legislation that is presented to the President.

options.text: Reconciliation automatically permits any AI policy provision.
options.explanation: Special restrictions, including the Byrd rule, limit what reconciliation may contain.

hint: Focus on Senate debate procedures, while remembering that content restrictions remain.
takeaway: Reconciliation changes the procedural route; it does not remove all legislative requirements.

sources.title: CRS: The Reconciliation Process — Frequently Asked Questions

prompt: An AI licensing proposal includes a small fee. Its sponsor argues that any revenue effect guarantees eligibility for reconciliation. What is the best response?

options.text: The Byrd rule prohibits every provision involving artificial intelligence.
options.explanation: The tests concern the provision’s budgetary and procedural characteristics, not the AI label.

options.text: Only the House applies the Byrd rule to reconciliation provisions.
options.explanation: The Byrd rule constrains reconciliation consideration in the Senate.

options.text: A merely incidental budget effect can still leave the provision vulnerable under the Byrd rule.
options.explanation: The Byrd rule examines more than whether a provision changes revenue at all.

options.text: Any fee makes all associated regulatory provisions automatically eligible.
options.explanation: A revenue connection does not by itself satisfy every Byrd-rule test.

hint: The relationship between the budget effect and the policy change matters.
takeaway: Adding a fee is not a universal way to fit regulatory policy into reconciliation.

sources.title: Senate Budget Committee: The Byrd Rule Explained

prompt: A House AI bill is considered under suspension of the rules. Which combination describes that procedure?

options.text: Unlimited debate, unrestricted amendments, and a simple-majority vote.
options.explanation: These are not the procedures governing House suspension motions.

options.text: No debate, automatic passage, and approval only by committee chairs.
options.explanation: The full House still acts; suspension does not delegate passage to committee chairs.

options.text: A 60-vote threshold, cloture petitions, and Senate-style debate.
options.explanation: Suspension is a House procedure; these features confuse it with Senate practice.

options.text: Limited debate, no floor amendments, and two-thirds support among members voting.
options.explanation: Suspension streamlines consideration but requires a two-thirds vote, with a quorum present.

hint: The faster route trades amendment opportunities for a higher voting threshold.
takeaway: A bipartisan House bill may use a different floor route from a contentious major package.

sources.title: House: Legislative process and floor consideration

prompt: The House adopts a structured rule for an AI bill. Your preferred amendment is not among those made in order. Under that rule, what should you expect?

options.text: The amendment is outside the set authorized for consideration.
options.explanation: Structured rules specify which amendments may be considered; relevance alone is insufficient.

options.text: Any member may offer it because it concerns the bill’s subject.
options.explanation: A structured rule can restrict even germane amendments to a specified list.

options.text: The amendment is automatically included in the bill without a vote.
options.explanation: Omission from the permitted list does not insert the amendment into legislative text.

options.text: The Senate must consider the amendment before the House can proceed.
options.explanation: The House rule governs its own floor consideration, not the Senate’s agenda.

hint: Look at the special rule and its accompanying list of permitted amendments.
takeaway: Rules Committee decisions can shape which policy alternatives receive a House vote.

sources.title: House Rules Committee: Special Rule Types

prompt: The House passes an AI bill. The Senate passes the same bill number but changes its reporting deadline. What must happen before presentation to the President?

options.text: The two deadlines both take effect and agencies choose one.
options.explanation: Neither conflicting version becomes law merely because each chamber passed a version.

options.text: Both chambers must agree to the same final text.
options.explanation: A difference in the deadline remains a legislative difference requiring resolution.

options.text: The Senate text automatically replaces the House text.
options.explanation: The Senate cannot unilaterally establish the text approved by both chambers.

options.text: The President chooses which chamber’s deadline to sign.
options.explanation: Congress must resolve the text before presenting the enrolled bill.

hint: The constitutional requirement concerns the same measure in the same form.
takeaway: Small textual differences matter just as much as large ones for bicameral agreement.

sources.title: House: Resolving Differences with the Senate

prompt: The House and Senate disagree over an AI provision. Must they always convene a conference committee to resolve the difference?

options.text: No; a joint press release is enough to settle the legal text.
options.explanation: Public agreement must still be translated into the necessary chamber actions.

options.text: Yes; the President must chair the conference committee.
options.explanation: Conferences involve members of Congress, and a conference is not the only route.

options.text: No; they can also exchange amendments until both agree to the same text.
options.explanation: Amendments between the chambers provide an alternative to a formal conference.

options.text: Yes; every disagreement requires a conference committee.
options.explanation: Congress can reconcile its positions without creating a formal conference committee.

hint: Consider the legislative “ping-pong” of amendments between chambers.
takeaway: The familiar conference-committee diagram is only one path to final agreement.

sources.title: House: Resolving Differences with the Senate

prompt: An AI bill was introduced in the 118th Congress but was never enacted before that Congress ended. What is required to pursue it as a bill in the 119th Congress?

options.text: Resume it automatically at the same committee stage and bill number.
options.explanation: A new Congress does not inherit pending bills as live legislation.

options.text: Ask the President to sign the expired introduced version.
options.explanation: An introduced, unenacted bill is not ready for presidential signature.

options.text: Obtain only a staff certification that its wording is unchanged.
options.explanation: Unchanged language does not remove the need for reintroduction and legislative action.

options.text: Reintroduce it and begin the legislative process under a new bill number.
options.explanation: An unenacted bill does not carry over from one Congress to the next.

hint: A Congress lasts two years; its pending bills do not continue indefinitely.
takeaway: Track the Congress number as part of a bill’s identity.

sources.title: Library of Congress: What happens to a bill at the end of a Congress?

prompt: It is November 2026, after the congressional election. A 119th-Congress AI bill has not been enacted or otherwise disposed of. Does the election alone make it expired?

options.text: No; the election does not itself end the sitting Congress.
options.explanation: Expiration at the end of a Congress is different from election day.

options.text: Yes; every pending bill expires when polls close.
options.explanation: The election does not terminate the current Congress’s pending legislation.

options.text: Yes; every bill automatically transfers to the next Congress as expired law.
options.explanation: An unenacted bill is not a law and does not transfer automatically.

options.text: No; the bill remains pending across all future Congresses.
options.explanation: Its life as a pending bill still ends when the Congress ends if it is not enacted.

hint: Distinguish an election from the end of the two-year Congress.
takeaway: Use the legislative calendar rather than election results to label a bill expired.

sources.title: Library of Congress: What happens to a bill at the end of a Congress?

prompt: The House passes an H.R. bill and the Senate passes its identically worded S. companion. Is that enough, by itself, to send a bill to the President?

options.text: No; companion bills can never become law.
options.explanation: One companion can become the common vehicle approved by both chambers.

options.text: No; both chambers must ultimately pass the same legislative vehicle.
options.explanation: Identical companion text is not enough until both chambers act on one common vehicle.

options.text: Yes; matching text automatically merges the two bill numbers.
options.explanation: Companion bills retain separate identities; there is no automatic merger.

options.text: Yes; whichever chamber voted last selects the final law number.
options.explanation: The last vote does not substitute for both chambers passing the same measure.

hint: Text and legislative vehicle are separate parts of the requirement.
takeaway: Follow the vehicle that actually crosses chambers and becomes law.

sources.title: House Legislative Counsel: Understanding the Legislative Process

prompt: You open an AI bill’s official document and see the heading “An Act.” Is that heading alone enough to conclude the proposal is law?

options.text: Yes; publication by GovInfo gives any proposal legal effect.
options.explanation: GovInfo publishes proposed bills as well as enacted laws.

options.text: No; Congress never uses that heading for enacted legislation.
options.explanation: Enacted legislation also uses the heading, so it cannot distinguish status by itself.

options.text: No; a bill can be styled “An Act” after passing only one chamber.
options.explanation: The heading can appear before enactment; check the action history and public-law record.

options.text: Yes; “An Act” always proves presidential signature.
options.explanation: The document’s heading is not proof that constitutional enactment requirements were completed.

hint: The title of the document is less informative than its version and enactment record.
takeaway: Read status metadata and the final law, not just a document’s opening words.

sources.title: CRS: Understanding Federal Legislation

prompt: The Senate adopts an AI incident-reporting amendment to a larger bill that has not yet passed. What has happened?

options.text: The amendment independently became a public law.
options.explanation: An amendment does not ordinarily become law independently of its legislative vehicle.

options.text: The House must automatically accept the amendment.
options.explanation: Senate amendment adoption does not bind the House to the same language.

options.text: The President can now sign the amendment by itself.
options.explanation: The measure must complete the required legislative steps before presentment.

options.text: The Senate changed the pending bill; the requirement is not yet federal law.
options.explanation: Amendment adoption is one step in consideration of the underlying measure.

hint: The amendment is attached to a legislative vehicle that is still moving.
takeaway: A successful amendment vote is not the same thing as enactment of its policy.

sources.title: GovInfo: Congressional Bills and version codes

prompt: A new AI law is signed today but states that one reporting duty takes effect 180 days after enactment. Which date governs that duty?

options.text: The specified date 180 days after enactment.
options.explanation: Congress can provide a later effective date for particular provisions.

options.text: Today, because all duties begin immediately upon signature.
options.explanation: An express delayed effective date controls the provision’s timing.

options.text: The bill’s introduction date, because that starts the legislative record.
options.explanation: Introduction does not create the legal duty or begin this statutory clock.

options.text: The next congressional election, regardless of the text.
options.explanation: The election is not the trigger stated in this law.

hint: Look for a provision-specific effective date rather than a single date for the whole act.
takeaway: Enactment, effective dates, and implementation deadlines can be different milestones.

sources.title: CRS: Understanding Federal Legislation

prompt: A hypothetical funding restriction applies only to money provided by a specified annual appropriations act. Which fact is essential before claiming it permanently bans an AI activity?

options.text: Whether the provision contains the phrase “artificial intelligence.”
options.explanation: The technology label does not establish duration or which spending is restricted.

options.text: The enacted restriction’s scope and duration, including which funds it covers.
options.explanation: A limitation on specified appropriated funds should not automatically be described as a permanent, universal ban.

options.text: Whether its sponsor calls it a permanent ban in a press release.
options.explanation: A sponsor’s description cannot replace the enacted language governing scope and duration.

options.text: Whether the restriction has more than ten cosponsors.
options.explanation: Cosponsor numbers do not determine the legal reach of an enacted funding limitation.

hint: Appropriations are defined by purpose, amount, and duration.
takeaway: Read funding restrictions precisely before turning them into broad policy claims.

sources.title: CRS: Appropriations Duration of Availability

prompt: An AI proposal has been referred to a committee but receives no hearings or markup. Which official generally has the committee’s primary agenda-setting authority?

options.text: The bill’s lead sponsor, even if not a committee member.
options.explanation: Sponsorship can help advocacy, but does not confer control of the committee’s agenda.

options.text: The ranking minority member, acting alone.
options.explanation: The ranking member leads the minority; primary committee agenda-setting authority generally lies with the chair.

options.text: The committee chair.
options.explanation: The chair generally decides which referred measures receive formal committee attention.

options.text: The chamber’s majority leader, rather than committee leadership.
options.explanation: Floor leadership influences priorities, but the question concerns primary agenda-setting inside a committee.

hint: Focus on the committee’s own leadership, not the proposal’s supporters.
takeaway: Referral creates an opportunity for consideration, not a promise of action.

sources.title: CRS: Introduction to the Legislative Process

prompt: A news report calls a senator the “ranking member” of a committee. What does that title usually mean?

options.text: The most senior majority-party member other than the chair.
options.explanation: The title identifies the leading minority member, not a second-ranking majority member.

options.text: The committee’s longest-serving member, regardless of party.
options.explanation: Seniority often matters, but the role is defined by leadership of the committee minority.

options.text: The minority leader of the entire chamber.
options.explanation: The chamber’s party leader and a committee’s ranking member are different positions.

options.text: The committee’s highest-ranking minority-party member.
options.explanation: The ranking member is the minority counterpart to the majority-party chair.

hint: The role is defined relative to the majority and minority on the committee.
takeaway: Committee leadership comes in majority and minority roles with different powers.

sources.title: Senate: Glossary

prompt: A bipartisan AI caucus endorses a bill. What does that endorsement establish?

options.text: An informal member group supports it; endorsement is not committee passage.
options.explanation: Caucuses can coordinate and advocate, but are distinct from legislative committees.

options.text: The bill has passed a standing committee by a recorded vote.
options.explanation: A caucus endorsement is not a standing committee’s legislative action.

options.text: All members of the caucus are automatically listed as bill cosponsors.
options.explanation: Joining a caucus and formally cosponsoring a bill are separate actions.

options.text: The endorsement legally binds each caucus member’s floor vote.
options.explanation: An informal caucus endorsement is not a legal instruction controlling members’ votes.

hint: An organization pursuing common legislative objectives is not necessarily a committee.
takeaway: Caucus activity can build a coalition without changing the bill’s official status.

sources.title: House Administration: Congressional Member Organizations

prompt: In May 2025, the House AI Whistleblower Protection Act (H.R. 3460) was referred to Education and Workforce. What is the best lesson from this referral?

options.text: The referral means the committee had already approved the bill.
options.explanation: Referral assigns a measure for consideration; it does not signify committee approval.

options.text: Committee jurisdiction follows the policy mechanism, including employment protections.
options.explanation: The bill addresses employment discrimination against whistleblowers, not simply AI technology in isolation.

options.text: Every bill mentioning AI is referred to this committee.
options.explanation: AI bills can address different policy areas and therefore different jurisdictions.

options.text: Only committees with “AI” in their names may handle AI legislation.
options.explanation: Congress uses existing subject-matter jurisdictions; a dedicated AI committee is not required.

hint: Ask what legal relationship the bill would regulate.
takeaway: “AI policy” crosses employment, commerce, defense, intelligence, and other jurisdictions.

sources.title: GovInfo: H.R. 3460, introduced version, May 15, 2025

prompt: An NDAA provision authorizes $50 million for an AI testing program but does not appropriate money. What should an implementation analyst check next?

options.text: Whether the committee report can substitute for enacted appropriations.
options.explanation: Report language alone does not create the missing budget authority.

options.text: Whether the President can treat the authorization as an automatic appropriation.
options.explanation: The distinction between authorization and budget authority remains after enactment.

options.text: Whether an appropriation or other available budget authority funds the program.
options.explanation: Authorization of appropriations does not itself supply the budget authority needed for spending.

options.text: Whether the agency can spend the full $50 million solely because it was authorized.
options.explanation: A funding authorization alone does not make that amount available to obligate.

hint: The question distinguishes permission to establish policy from authority to spend money.
takeaway: Follow both the authorizing legislation and the funding path.

sources.title: CRS: FY2025 NDAA — Overview of Funding Authorizations

prompt: An appropriations committee report asks an agency to publish an AI evaluation framework. The direction is not incorporated into statutory text. Which assessment is most accurate?

options.text: It is automatically identical in legal force to an enacted statutory command.
options.explanation: A report is not itself a statute; incorporation and other legal context can matter.

options.text: It has no relevance because agencies never respond to committee reports.
options.explanation: Agencies often seek to comply because report language communicates congressional expectations.

options.text: It becomes binding whenever the committee chair repeats it in a speech.
options.explanation: A public statement does not transform report language into statutory text.

options.text: It can exert significant oversight pressure but generally lacks the force of statutory text.
options.explanation: Report directions matter politically and administratively, but are generally not binding in the same way as law.

hint: Distinguish practical congressional influence from the legal source of a duty.
takeaway: Separate enacted requirements from committee expectations when assessing implementation.

sources.title: CRS: Appropriations Report Language

prompt: Congress has enacted an AI security law. An agency misses a required implementation deadline. Which activity is an example of congressional oversight?

options.text: Holding a hearing to examine the delay and agency implementation.
options.explanation: Committees use oversight hearings to review how executive agencies administer legislation.

options.text: Treating the missed deadline as automatic repeal of the law.
options.explanation: A missed deadline does not by itself establish that the law has been repealed.

options.text: Allowing a committee press release to replace the statute.
options.explanation: A press release cannot amend the law governing implementation.

options.text: Requiring every oversight hearing to enact a new bill.
options.explanation: Oversight can investigate implementation without producing new legislation.

hint: Congress’s work does not end when a bill becomes law.
takeaway: Oversight tests whether enacted policy is being carried out as intended.

sources.title: Senate: Committee hearings and oversight

prompt: CBO estimates the budgetary effects of an AI proposal. What should you infer about CBO’s position on whether Congress should enact it?

options.text: Publishing the estimate makes CBO a cosponsor.
options.explanation: Congressional sponsorship and nonpartisan budget analysis are different roles.

options.text: The estimate is analysis, not a policy endorsement.
options.explanation: CBO does not recommend which policies Congress should enact.

options.text: A positive spending estimate means CBO recommends passage.
options.explanation: Estimated spending does not indicate an endorsement.

options.text: A deficit increase means CBO has formally vetoed the bill.
options.explanation: CBO analyzes legislation; it does not have a veto over it.

hint: A score describes expected effects; elected lawmakers make value judgments.
takeaway: Use CBO to understand fiscal consequences without attributing a political recommendation.

sources.title: Congressional Budget Office: Processes

prompt: A congressional committee wants an independent examination of whether agencies are implementing AI procurement safeguards effectively. Which congressional support agency is especially suited to that audit role?

options.text: The Office of Management and Budget (OMB).
options.explanation: OMB is part of the executive branch, not a congressional support agency.

options.text: The National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST).
options.explanation: NIST is an executive-branch technical agency, not Congress’s audit institution.

options.text: The Government Accountability Office (GAO).
options.explanation: GAO conducts evaluations and audits supporting congressional oversight of government performance.

options.text: The Congressional Budget Office (CBO).
options.explanation: CBO specializes in budget and economic analysis rather than this implementation-audit role.

hint: Look for Congress’s institution focused on government accountability and program performance.
takeaway: Congress can use GAO investigations to test implementation claims.

sources.title: GAO: What GAO Does

prompt: An AI bill wins overwhelming support in committee. Why might it still receive no floor vote?

options.text: Committee approval automatically removes a bill from consideration.
options.explanation: Reporting a bill normally advances it toward possible consideration; it does not defeat it.

options.text: Only the President may schedule congressional floor votes.
options.explanation: Floor proceedings are controlled within Congress, not by presidential scheduling authority.

options.text: Every committee-reported bill must first win a national referendum.
options.explanation: Federal bills do not require a national referendum before floor consideration.

options.text: Committee approval does not guarantee a place on the chamber’s floor agenda.
options.explanation: Committee recommendations are important, but floor scheduling and chamber procedures remain separate hurdles.

hint: Committee action and chamber agenda control occur at different institutional levels.
takeaway: A strong committee vote is evidence of progress, not a guaranteed route to enactment.

sources.title: Senate: About the Committee System
CRS: Introduction to the Legislative Process

prompt: You want to discuss the substance of an AI bill with a representative’s office. Which staff role most commonly tracks legislation in an assigned policy portfolio?

options.text: A legislative assistant or aide covering that issue.
options.explanation: Legislative assistants commonly follow assigned issues and prepare policy and hearing work for the member.

options.text: The communications director handling press coverage.
options.explanation: Communications staff explain the member’s positions publicly, but are not ordinarily the assigned legislative portfolio staff.

options.text: The scheduler arranging the member’s meetings.
options.explanation: A scheduler can arrange access; that role does not by itself identify the policy specialist.

options.text: The district caseworker handling individual agency problems.
options.explanation: Constituent casework and legislative portfolio analysis are related but distinct office functions.

hint: Ask which staffer covers the issue, because office titles and assignments can vary.
takeaway: Policy expertise often sits with staff; verify each office’s actual portfolio assignments.

sources.title: House: Compensation and Diversity Study — staff responsibilities

prompt: Congress agrees to a concurrent budget resolution containing fiscal targets. Has the resolution itself become a public law funding an AI program?

options.text: No; only the President may write congressional fiscal targets.
options.explanation: Congress develops and agrees to its own budget resolution.

options.text: No; a budget resolution guides congressional budgeting and is not signed into law.
options.explanation: Congress uses the resolution as a fiscal framework; spending legislation must supply the relevant authority.

options.text: Yes; every concurrent resolution becomes law without further steps.
options.explanation: Concurrent resolutions are not presented to the President as public laws.

options.text: Yes; its fiscal targets automatically appropriate each agency’s funding.
options.explanation: A budget framework is distinct from legislation providing budget authority.

hint: Compare a congressional budget framework with an enacted appropriations measure.
takeaway: A budget resolution, an authorization, and an appropriation perform different jobs.

sources.title: Senate Budget Committee: Committee History and Responsibilities
